verdicts.reason: The complete statement matches the cited Core statement word for word. It keeps the condition ("If multiple matching text sequences remain after processing the prefix, exact text and suffix"), the source and version (W3C 2017 Web Annotation Data Model, 2017-02-23 Recommendation, section 4.2.4), and the modal strength ("recommends", not "requires"). The heading "W3C quote selection can match multiple sequences" is a shortened form. Its "can" covers the conditional case and doesn't claim the selector always matches several sequences. Nothing is missing, misattributed or overstated.

Block 169 says "This use of multiple place elements should be distinguished from the (possibly simpler) case where a number of places with some property in common are being grouped together for convenience, for example, in a gazetteer". "This use" points back to the hierarchical Carmarthen example in Block 167. Block 169 also says listPlace "is provided as a means of grouping places together where there is no implication that the grouped elements constitute a distinct place". The statement matches both clauses, including the hedge "possibly simpler" and the gazetteer example.

Block 171 contains every clause in the statement. It speaks of many kinds of information beyond name and location, and of likely project-specific categories. It says "As with persons therefore these Guidelines make no claim to comprehensiveness". It says the generic state, trait and event elements should be used instead, each customizable via its type attribute. It adds that they are complemented by predefined elements of general utility, and its specList names population, climate and terrain.

Block 175 supports all three parts. First, state, trait "and others of the same class, can be nested hierarchically", and when this is done type values "are to be understood as cumulatively inherited". Second, "responsibility is not an additive property, and therefore an element either states it explicitly, or inherits it from its nearest ancestor". Third, "Dating is slightly different again, in that a child element may specify a date more precisely than its parent". Nothing is overstated and no condition is lost.

Block 179 says the "so-called stand-off" style "has the advantage that we can now also represent the fact that a place may be a 'part of' more than one other place; for example, Réunion is part of France, as well as part of the Mascarenes". Once a France declaration is added, it models "this dual allegiance by means of a relation element": <relation name="partOf" active="#REN" passive="#FRA #MASC"/>. That is one identifier in active and two in passive, as the statement says. Leaving out the step of adding France does not make any part of the statement wrong.

Block 182 says: "An event is a change of state whether real, planned, fictional, or purported about which more information is known." It says eventName "may be used to encode the proper name of an event, if known". It says head or label "may also appear in event, either in lieu of or in addition to the eventName element, to provide a human-readable heading or editorially supplied label for the event". The statement follows each clause faithfully.

Block 183 says: "These guidelines do not prescribe what encoders count as events, nor their granularity, nesting, or amount of other information to record in relation to each event. Yet most events can be identified by their time, location, or agents involved (be they organizations, persons, or objects)." The statement restates this accurately, keeping the limit "most events".

Block 184 says an event element "may be used to record information about a place, person, or organization related to the described event; for this reason the element may appear as content of a place, person, or org". It says events can also be described "independently of either a place, person, or organization". It says this "may be useful not only for encoding texts which describe named events and their eventNames, but also in applications as chronologies or lists of significant events". The statement matches, and dropping the parenthetical examples changes nothing.

Block 205 begins "So far we have discussed ways in which a name or referring string ... may be resolved by considering the object that the name refers to". The resolution is "effected by means of the key or ref attributes available to all elements which are members of the att.naming class". It goes on to say that names "can also be regarded as objects in their own right, irrespective of the objects to which they are attached, notably in onomastic studies". It uses "nym" for "the canonical or normalized form of a name regarded in such a way", and its specList names listNym and nym. The statement matches all of this.

Block 206 says "Any element which is a member of the att.naming class may use the attribute nymRef to indicate the nym with which it corresponds". Its example is <nym xml:id="N123"><form>Antony</form></nym> together with <forename nymRef="#N123">Tony</forename> in running text. It notes that "this association (between 'Tony' and 'Antony') has nothing to do with any individual who might use the name". The statement's account of the example and the note is accurate.

Block 209 says "Because a schema intending to make use of the nym or listNym element must include the dictionaries module as well as the namesdates module, many other elements are available in addition to form". Its example is "to provide a more complex etymological decomposition of a name, we might use the existing etym element". The statement gets the requirement and the result right. It drops "more complex", but that does not distort the claim.

Block 212 says nym "may also combine a number of other nym elements together, where it is intended to show that they are all regarded as variations on the same root", and shows the forms of John as a hierarchic structure. In the example, form xml:lang="la" is Iohannes, "en" is John, "ru" is Ivan and "fr" is Jean. The two nyms nested inside J450 (the John nym), J4501 Johnny and J4502 Jon, have form elements with no xml:lang. The statement describes this exactly.

Block 243 contains <moduleSpec xml:id="DND" ident="namesdates">. Inside it are <idno type="FPI">Names, dates, persons and places</idno> and <desc xml:lang="en" versionDate="2006-09-13">Names and dates</desc>. The statement gives the module ident, the FPI value and the English description correctly.

The Terms entry is a bare label that makes no substantive claim. The Open questions are explicit questions. The Appraisal's statement that the chapter sorts its methods into conformant, extension and non-conformant matches b11, b16, b18, b20, b21, b36, b38, b45 and b49. The Appraisal keeps those judgements attributed to the chapter and disclaims any independent measurement. The release, language and identity details come only from the acquisition metadata. Block 115 contains <moduleSpec xml:id="DDS" ident="textstructure"> within the chapter's module paragraph and ends: "The selection and combination of modules to form a TEI schema is described in <ptr target="#STIN"/>." Both parts of the statement match: the module ident and the pointer to STIN.

Block 2 says the module encodes names and phrases descriptive of persons, places or organizations "in a manner more detailed than that possible using the elements already provided ... in the Core module". It says the core elements mark a proper noun or referring string and give the kind of object "only by supplying a value for the type attribute". It says this module's elements "supply a detailed sub-structure" and "distinguish explicitly between names of persons, places, and organizations". The statement keeps every part, including the 'only' limitation.

Block 3 says the module also provides elements for information about the referent and to represent the name "independently of its application". It says that where the core module "allows one simply to represent" that text is a name, this module further represents personal name, person and canonical name. It names as main intended applications biographical, historical or geographical data systems such as gazetteers and biographical databases "where these are to be integrated with encoded texts". Rendering "simply" as "only" matches the source's contrast with "further".

Block 8 supports every clause. att.naming is a subclass of att.canonical and inherits key and ref, which are "two different ways of associating any sort of name with its referent". role is for minimal information such as occupation or status. The additional attribute (nymRef in the specList) associates the name with a base or canonical form. ref "should be used wherever it is possible to supply a direct link such as a URI". ref="#DPB1" "requires that there exist somewhere a person element with the identifier DPB1", which "might alternatively be provided by some other document" through a URI. "More than one URI may be supplied if the name refers to more than one person."

Block 9 provides key "for cases where no such direct link is required", because of local-convention resolution or because "the encoder judges that no such resolution is necessary". It illustrates the first case with a local database accessed by "some system-specific identifier constructed in a project-specific way from the value supplied for the key attribute". It illustrates the second with country or airport codes "which it is probably unnecessary for an encoder to expand further". The hedge 'probably' is kept.

Block 10 says: "However, as explained in <ptr target="#CONARS"/>, interchange is improved by use of tag URIs in ref instead of key." Both the claim and the pointer to another section for the explanation are in the text.

Block 11 says: "The nymRef attribute has a more specialized use, where it is the name itself which is of interest rather than the person, place, or organization being named." The statement paraphrases this faithfully.

Block 26 says the core rs and name elements "can distinguish names in a text but are insufficiently powerful to mark their internal components or structure". It says that for nominal record linkage "or even to create an alphabetically sorted list of personal names, it is important to distinguish between a family name, a forename and an honorary title". Its specList gives persName, surname, forename, roleName, addName, nameLink and genName as "provided for these and related purposes".

Block 28 says persName "may be used in preference to the general name element irrespective of whether or not the components of the personal name are also to be marked". It says persName is synonymous with name type="person" except that its type attribute allows subcategorization (married, birth, pen, pseudo, religious). "Consequently the following examples are equivalent": rs type="person" with ref, name inside rs type="person" with ref on the rs, name type="person" with ref, and persName with ref, all with the same tag URI. Relying on the commented-out text was not needed.

Block 31 says type "may be used with both forename and surname elements to provide further culture- or project-specific detail". It says values "are not constrained, and may be chosen as appropriate to the encoding needs of the project" and "may be used to distinguish different kinds of forename or surname, as well as to indicate the function a name component fills within the whole". Its example marks a surname type="toponymic" with ref="#dystvold" pointing to the placeName from which it derives.

Block 35 says patronymics "may be treated as forenames". It says "When a patronymic is used as a surname, however (e.g. by an individual who otherwise would have no surname, but lives in a culture which requires surnames), it may be tagged as such". It says "Alternatively" one may use addName as "a distinct kind of name, neither a forename nor a surname", and gives an example where type on forename (type="patronym") "distinguish[es] a patronymic from other forenames". The surname option's condition is kept.

Block 39 says addName and roleName "are used to mark all name components other than those already listed". It says roleName "encloses an associated name component such as an aristocratic or official title which exists in some sense independently of its bearer" and "The distinction is not always a clear one". It says a person's role in context (witness, defendant in a legal document) "should not be encoded using the roleName element", which marks "roles which function as part of a person's name". It says "Information about roles, occupations, etc. of a person are encoded within the person element".

Block 42 says almost word for word that these 'highly flexible' mechanisms 'will not cater for every personal name, nor for every processing need'. It also recommends feature structures 'as the most appropriate mechanism' where internal structure 'is highly complex or where name components are particularly ambiguous'. Both conditions are kept in the statement.

Block 45 defines 'organization' as 'any named collection of people regarded as a single unit'. Its examples include institutions and businesses, plus racial or ethnic groupings or political factions 'where these are regarded as forming a single agency', and the statement keeps that condition. It also says naming such groups 'often serves a particular political or social agenda', that analysing such phrases 'may therefore be of considerable importance to the social historian', and that this holds even where an organization's existence is harder to show than that of a named person. The statement's 'may matter' is weaker than the source, not an overstatement.

Block 46 says organizational names 'can be marked up as referring strings or as proper names with the rs or name elements respectively'. It says orgName 'is provided for use where it is desired to distinguish organizational names more explicitly' and 'is a member of the same attribute classes as persName'. Each part of the statement matches, including which element goes with which role.

Block 47 calls the orgName encoding 'equivalent to, but more specific than, either of the following representations', which are the rs version (with a nested name) and the name version. It says orgName, 'like the rs and name elements', has a key attribute for an external identifier such as a database key, and a ref attribute to 'point directly to an org element containing information about the organization itself'. It also says type 'should be used to characterize the name (rather than the organization)', with acronym, phrase and composite examples. Describing the first version simply as 'rs' is a fair summary.

Block 52 says place names 'can simply be marked up with the rs element, or with the name element', like other proper nouns or noun phrases used as names. It says that for cartographers and historical geographers the component parts 'provide important information about the relation between the name and some spot in space and time', and 'also provide important evidence in historical linguistics'. Dropping 'important' in the last clause weakens rather than overstates the source.

Block 53 says the Guidelines 'distinguish three ways of referring to places'. It describes placeName as possibly holding 'one or more names for hierarchically-organized geo-political or administrative units', and geogName as for places named 'simply in terms of geographical features such as mountains or rivers'. It says relational expressions 'may itself be regarded as a way of referring to a place, and hence as a kind of named place'. The statement follows all three closely and keeps the 'may'.

Block 55 says placeName, 'like the persName element', 'may be regarded simply as an abbreviation' for name type="place" or rs type="place", and that 'the following encodings are thus equivalent'. Its footnote says 'Strictly, a suitable value such as figurative should be added to the two place names which are presented periphrastically in the second version' (the placeName version). The footnote adds that this would 'preserve the distinction indicated by the choice of rs rather than name' in the first version. The statement gets the modal wording, which version is meant, and the footnote's purpose right.

Block 67 says place-name structure is 'like that of personal names—complex and subject to an enormous amount of variation across time and different cultures'. It says the recommendations 'should however be adequate for a majority of users and applications' and 'may be extended using the mechanisms described in chapter MD to add new elements to the existing classes'. It says the NDNYM elements 'may also be of use' when the focus is on name components, and 'Alternatively, the meaning structure itself may be represented using feature structures'. All the hedges survive in the statement.

Block 82 says the Guidelines 'propose a flexible strategy, in which encoders may choose for themselves the approach appropriate to their needs'. Its example: someone converting DNB-type records who wants to keep the text as is could have person 'simply contain the text of an article, placed within p elements, possibly using elements such as name or date'. For 'a more structured entry', one 'would extract the data and place information contained in the text, and encode it directly using the more specific elements described in this section'. The statement matches, including the hypothetical framing.

Block 84 says such information 'essentially comprises a series of statements or assertions' about four things. These are traits 'which do not, by and large, change over time', states 'which hold true only at a specific time', and 'events or incidents which may lead to a change of state or, less frequently, trait'.
